summary: Offers advice on how to host a successful IETF Birds-of-a-Feather session, particularly one aimed at forming a working group, based on the experience of the authors with many BOFs that worked or failed. This is an informational document.

eli5.summary: Before a new club can start, people hold a first meeting. This memo gives tips for making that first meeting go well.

questions: how to run a successful ietf bof
how to form an ietf working group
do you need a bof to form a working group
subtitle: Practical advice from experience on preparing, running and following up an IETF Birds-of-a-Feather session.

tldr.problem: Many IETF Birds-of-a-Feather (BOF) sessions fail because organizers start too late, argue about solutions instead of the problem, or ask poor questions in the room.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lays out an ideal ten-step path: shape the problem with a small group, consult Area Directors, build a public community and mailing list, agree on a charter, then hold a tightly focused BOF with well-prepared questions.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational guidance, not a rule. It also notes that no process requirement demands a BOF before a working group is formed.

facts.label: BOF scheduling deadline
facts.value: About six weeks before the IETF meeting

today: RFC 5434 is an Informational RFC and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It is guidance rather than a requirement, and it says no BOF is strictly required to form a working group.

sections.title: What a BOF Is For
sections.content:
A BOF is a Birds-of-a-Feather session held at an IETF meeting. Some are one-shot presentations or open meetings on a problem with a document that has no active working group. In many cases, though, the aim is to form a Working Group (WG).

For that aim, the BOF has to show the community agrees on five things: there is a problem and the IETF is the right place to solve it; enough people will do the work; the scope and deliverables are well defined; the deliverables are the right set; and the group has a reasonable chance of finishing its charter in time. More background on WGs and BOFs is in RFC 2418.
sections.eli5: A BOF is a first meeting to see if enough people care about a problem to start a team. The meeting has to show everyone agrees what the job is and that there are helpers.

sections.title: The Recommended Steps
sections.content:
The RFC describes an ideal ten-step sequence. Most of it is public discussion, so that much of the work happens on a mailing list before the BOF rather than in the room.

  • A small group privately shapes a problem statement, checks whether an existing WG already covers it, consults WGs and area mailing lists, and writes Internet Drafts. Drafts that explain the problem are worth more than drafts that propose solutions.
  • The group may informally float the idea to an Area Director (AD). When unsure which area fits, approach several ADs at about the same time and tell each who else you are talking to. The RFC calls "AD shopping" counterproductive.
  • Create a public mailing list, post a call for participation, and hold substantive discussion centered on the problem statement.
  • Submit the formal BOF request, with an agenda, expected attendance and conflicts to avoid. Without at least one Internet Draft, asking an AD to approve a BOF is generally pointless.
  • In the weeks before the meeting, focus on areas of disagreement, iterate on a proposed charter, and settle the questions to be asked at the BOF.
  • At the meeting, brief the presenters beforehand, and consider the WG chair training tutorials.

Timing matters. The deadline to schedule a BOF is about six weeks before the IETF meeting, so preparation should begin 3 to 4 months ahead, around the meeting before the one you want.
sections.eli5: It is like planning a school club: first a few friends decide the idea, then you ask a teacher, then you tell the whole school and listen, and only then you book the room. Start early, because the room booking closes weeks ahead.

sections.title: Understand the Real Problem
sections.content:
The RFC says the key issue in chartering new work is agreeing on the real, underlying problem faced by the customer, operator or deployer of a technology. Some WGs have produced output that was not adopted because the operator's real problem was never understood.

Arguments about competing solutions can also stalemate a WG or BOF. Often they are proxies for the unresolved question of whether an approach addresses the problem at all. The best description of the problem usually comes from the operators who must deploy the solution, so their voice should shape the problem statement.
sections.eli5: If you build a bridge before asking where people actually need to cross, nobody uses it. Ask the people with the problem first.

sections.title: Running the BOF and Following Up
sections.content:
The organizer should know in advance by what criteria the BOF will count as successful. If the goal is a WG, everything should lead to one answer: does the room agree that the IETF should form a WG with this specific charter? Presentations that do not support that goal should be left out.

The RFC lists useful questions to ask the room, such as whether there is support for the charter, whether the problem is clear, well scoped, solvable and useful to solve, who will review documents, who will edit them, and how many people feel a WG should not be formed. It recommends floating the questions on the mailing list and to the ADs first.

Afterwards, assess the result with the ADs. If it went well, finalize the charter on the BOF mailing list and ask the IESG to consider it; the IESG usually posts the proposed charter to the IETF list and decides partly on feedback. If more work is needed, a second and final BOF is possible, but expectations are higher and it must show all earlier issues are resolved.
sections.eli5: In the meeting, keep asking one simple question: should we start this team, with this job description? Afterwards, check how it went and decide whether to start or try once more.

sections.title: Pitfalls, Chairing and Whether a BOF Is Needed
sections.content:
The RFC lists six pitfalls seen repeatedly: starting too late; focusing on solutions instead of the problem; asking the wrong questions (for example, asking people to approve a charter they have not seen on the mailing list); poor advertising, such as a cute but unintuitive BOF name; giving agenda time to off-purpose presentations; and poor time management.

On chairing, organizers should not assume they will chair the BOF or the eventual WG. ADs may choose more experienced chairs or co-chairs, since people driving a technology often do best focusing on the technical work.

There is no actual process requirement to hold a BOF before forming a WG. The requirement is that the IESG, with the sponsoring AD or ADs, approves a formal charter as described in RFC 2418. BOFs are a tool for engaging the community and producing an acceptable charter.
sections.eli5: Common mistakes are showing up late, arguing about gadgets instead of the problem, and letting people talk too long. And you do not strictly need the first meeting at all if everyone already agrees.

references.text: Bradner, S., "IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures", BCP 25, RFC 2418, September 1998.
